lead.title: Real rates, political dollars and predictions on the record
paras: Round 5 worked through the fifteen open questions on the Landscape page, audited the project's memory and wrote down dated predictions before the events they describe. The biggest answer is about interest rates. The real 10-year Treasury yield rose 73bp from end 2025 to 2.66% on 23 October, and almost none of the move was expected inflation. The court's reading is a Fed expected to stay tight while it fights oil-driven inflation in an AI-fed boom (about 35bp), plus a push from Japan (about 18bp), with the term premium and direct AI crowding-out smaller. The accord Kevin Warsh has floated would shrink the Fed, not cap yields, so the desk cuts the odds of an explicit yield cap by 2035 from 25 to 15. The corporate tax hole closes when AI investment stops growing, and the 'flat producer prices' puzzle turned out to be a mislabelled food series.

Crisis dollars are becoming political. Japan paid for both of its 2026 yen defenses by selling dollar securities and never touched the Fed's FIMA line. No Gulf state has a US dollar line, and the Treasury fund that would provide one has $24.9B of dollar securities behind its $219B headline, because most of it is IMF reserve assets matched by liabilities. Central banks without a standing Fed line are the ones buying gold, and more of them now store it at home. About two thirds of dollar stablecoins are held outside the US. China grows the yuan through refinancing, panda bonds and 32 swap agreements rather than solar loans.

In Europe, Moody's held France at Aa3 negative on 23 October, so the desk's 70 against a thin market's 87.5 to 90.5 on a downgrade by 31 October is recorded as a pending score. A one-notch cut would have mattered little. Official fiscal studies agree that route of entry, age at arrival and earnings decide what new residents contribute, and Europeans are not moving to Latin America or Southeast Asia in rising shares. At home, US housing supply is shrinking under 7% mortgages, and the newsletter's 'borrow at 6.19%, earn 13.6%' adds little to the typical outcome while a 50% loan faces a 35% to 52% chance of a margin call over 10 to 20 years.

The scenario odds stay at 62/15/1/22, 44/23/3/30 and 31/28/10/31, with the neutral layer still shown as 13/17/18 for gold and Bitcoin and 2/6/10 for multipolar fiat. Five new conditional rules (C7 to C11) say what would move them. The desk wrote 72 dated predictions with resolution rules, and the memory audit confirmed 38 of 52 recalled figures and corrected six, none of which moves the odds.

groups.title: Why real rates rose, whether the Fed will cap yields, and where the corporate tax went
groups.intro: The 2026 rise in real rates is mostly a hawkish Fed in an oil-hit, AI-fed economy, plus Japan. The accord Warsh wants would shrink the Fed, not cap yields. The corporate tax hole closes when AI capex stops growing, and the 'flat producer prices' puzzle was a mislabelled series.

items.q: Is the 2026 rise in real interest rates driven by AI capital demand, or by oil, Japan and the term premium?
a: Mostly by a higher expected path for US policy rates, with Japan as the clearest outside push, while oil, the term premium and AI are each smaller pieces. From 31 December 2025 to 23 October 2026 the 10-year Treasury yield rose 82bp (4.18% to 5.00%) and the inflation-protected, or real, 10-year yield rose 73bp (1.93% to 2.66%, peak 2.95% on 5 October), while expected inflation (the breakeven) rose only 9bp. So 2026 was a real-rate move, not an inflation scare. The desk's central split of the 73bp is: the Fed path in a strong, oil-hit economy about 35bp (range 30 to 40), Japan and global spillover about 18bp (15 to 20), term premium and fiscal supply about 10bp (0 to 20) and direct AI crowding-out about 10bp (5 to 15). AI matters mostly indirectly, by feeding the strong growth that lets a hawkish Fed hike.

The two term structure models the Fed itself publishes disagree. The New York Fed's ACM model puts the whole rise in expected short rates (+87bp) with the term premium flat (0.75% to 0.72%). The Board's Kim-Wright model splits it about half and half (term premium 0.57% to 0.99%, its highest since 2010). The court treats the term premium share as 0 to 40bp until a survey-based check settles it. A daily regression on named drivers (a model, with low explanatory power) gives Japan about 17bp (the Japanese 10-year yield rose from 2.07% to 2.91%), oil about 10bp (Brent $60.8 to $111.7, which mostly lifted breakevens), an AI stock proxy about zero, and about 47bp unexplained, which is where the Fed path, fiscal supply and AI capital demand sit.

AI capital demand is real and large: the four biggest spenders' cash capex was $294.8B in the first half of 2026, up 84% on a year earlier (SEC filings). It shows up as growth and as a higher long-run expected rate (ACM's 5-year rate five years ahead rose 61bp), not as a daily price factor. The earlier Landscape figure of '82bp to 2.76%' was right for 21 October against 2 January. The court's house figure is +73bp to 2.66% at the 23 October close. Either way the AI dividend does nothing for the debt ratio while real rates rise with growth.

v.g: The bond market charges a higher real price for money because the Fed is expected to stay tight, so fiscal relief from lower rates is not on offer while oil and growth stay high.
v.b: Plan on real borrowing costs near 2.5% to 3% for ten years, and allow for the term premium part to rise if the Kim-Wright model is right.
v.p: Mortgage and car-loan rates are high because the Fed is fighting fuel-driven inflation in a strong economy, not because investors fear a US default.

items.q: Will the 2028 Fed leadership turnover bring a Fed-Treasury accord on yields?
a: Probably not an accord that caps yields. Some kind of accord is likely to be discussed, but the one Kevin Warsh has floated points the other way: a joint Fed and Treasury statement on the Fed's balance sheet and on Treasury's issuance, so the Fed can shrink its footprint, which he says would not mean a return to pre-1951 practice. Desk odds: a Warsh-style balance-sheet accord by end 2028, 25. An explicit cap or ceiling on Treasury yields, 3 by end 2028 and 15 by 2035 (down from 25). Fed long-end yield support with yield language after the 2028 turnover, 30 by 2032 (the Round 3 bundled figure of 40 was retired by the decode panel). A bond-market episode that forces Fed balance-sheet action stays at 45 by 2035.

The 2028 turnover is a change of Board majority, not of chair. Warsh's chair term runs to 2030-05-21 and his governor seat to 2040. Trump appointees hold 3 of 7 seats (Warsh, Bowman, Waller). Jefferson's vice-chair term ends in September 2027 and Powell's governor term on 2028-01-31, so a fourth appointee gives a Trump-appointed majority by early 2028 even if Lisa Cook stays. Rate decisions still need 7 of 12 FOMC votes, and the Warsh FOMC has been hawkish.

History cuts against a cap without a crisis. The 1942 peg held bills at 3/8% and long bonds near 2.5% until consumer prices rose 17.6% in a year (1946 to 1947) and at a 21% annual rate in February 1951, and the 4 March 1951 Accord ended the cap. Today Treasury already manages duration itself through bills (22.4% of marketable debt) and long-end buybacks of at least $4B per operation, which substitutes for a cap. A cap needs a different chain: a disorderly 30-year auction or bond volatility far above normal, plus a dovish Board. Conditional C7 records what would move the scenario odds.

v.g: The live design is a smaller Fed, with Treasury managing duration and regulation creating captive buyers. That is repression by plumbing, not by peg.
v.b: Buying long bonds ahead of a yield cap has weak support before a disorderly episode. Watch FOMC and refunding texts for any yield level.
v.p: A cap would only come after a crisis or with a much more dovish Fed, and its cost would be inflation above savings rates for years, as in 1946 to 1951.

items.q: Does the corporate tax collapse reverse when AI capex growth slows?
a: Yes, mostly, because the drag comes from the growth of AI investment, not its level, and two of its parts are one-offs that are already fading. Net federal corporate receipts fell from $529.9B (FY2024) to $452.1B (FY2025) and $381.4B (FY2026). The 2025 law made 100% bonus depreciation permanent and restored immediate expensing of domestic research, with a catch-up of 2022 to 2024 amounts, which nearly doubled refunds in FY2026 ($34.3B to $61.5B). The desk's timing model puts the big-four expensing drag at about $43B in 2026, peaking near $55B in 2027 if capex grows another 25%, then shrinking to about $5B to $12B by 2030 once capex goes flat. The deferred tax is not paid back while investment continues, but the annual hole closes.

The fall was front-loaded. Receipts fell 28% from October to March but only 8.6% from April to September, and September 2026 was up 38% on a year earlier. The three hyperscalers that report it show current federal tax falling from $32.7B to $6.5B in a year (Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, SEC filings). Alphabet has said 2027 capex will rise 'significantly', so the drag likely peaks in 2027.

Dated tests replace the old one: FY2027 net corporate receipts above FY2026's $381.4B, desk 65. The corporate share of federal receipts above 9% in FY2028, desk 40, rising to about 60 if 2027 capex guidance comes in flat. Both are in the pre-registration ledger.

v.g: Do not budget on a permanent 7% corporate share, and do not expect the lost years back either. Expensing defers tax for as long as capex grows.
v.b: The cash-tax holiday ends when capex stops growing, not when it stops, so a plateau in 2027 or 2028 raises cash taxes within one to three years.
v.p: Workers carried more of the federal tax load while the AI boom ran (individual and payroll taxes were 86.2% of receipts), and that tilt eases only after the boom levels off.

items.q: Why was producer price inflation for finished consumer goods flat in 2026 while energy CPI rose 20.4%?
a: It was not flat. The puzzle came from a mislabelled series. The series the project used, WPUFD4111, is 'Finished Consumer Foods' (the court checked the official title), not finished consumer goods, and food prices at the producer level were indeed flat (minus 0.9% on a year in September 2026, index 283.977). Producer energy actually rose more than consumer energy: the producer price index for final demand energy was up 35.4% on a year, gasoline 64.3%, diesel about 115%, and finished goods in total 8.4%.

Energy CPI rose 'only' 20.4% because about half of it is electricity and piped gas, which rose 4.4% and 5.0% under regulated and contract pricing. Consumer energy goods rose 35.3%, almost exactly in line with producer energy (35.4%). Wholesale natural gas fell while oil products soared, which kept power and gas bills near 5%.

The real gap worth watching is in everyday goods. Producer prices for finished consumer goods excluding food and energy rose 4.0% while consumer core goods prices rose only 0.7%. A stronger dollar (index 98.28 to 101.75 this year), import prices for consumer goods up only 2.7% before duties, and squeezed margins between factory and shelf explain the gap. If stores rebuild margins in 2027, core goods inflation rises. That is the pipeline risk.

v.g: The 2026 shock is visible in producer prices, so the Fed is right to treat it as broad, not as a consumer-only quirk.
v.b: Retailers and importers are holding a margin squeeze of about 3 points on core goods that they will try to pass on in 2027.
v.p: Fuel rose about a third and power bills about 5%. The next wave, if it comes, is in everyday goods as stores rebuild margins.

groups.title: Who gets dollars in a crisis, who holds them on new rails, and what China offers instead
groups.intro: Dollar stablecoins are mostly held abroad. Japan sells Treasuries instead of borrowing. The Gulf has no US line, and the Treasury's fund has only about $25B of dollar securities. Central banks without a Fed line buy gold, and China grows the yuan through debt deals, not solar loans.

items.q: Who actually holds dollar stablecoins, country by country?
a: Nobody publishes a country table, so the honest answer is a range by region. On the desk's model about two thirds of the $304.5B of dollar stablecoins is held outside the US (central 68%, range 59% to 78%, about $208B) and about $96B inside it (range $66B to $126B). An IMF working paper of 2 October 2026 covering 188 countries puts about three quarters with emerging and developing economies, at the top of the desk's range because it attributes exchange balances by web traffic and misses US institutions. By region the central estimates are Asia-Pacific about $94B, Europe including Turkey, Russia and Ukraine about $46B, Africa and the Middle East about $35B, and Latin America about $33B. Country names inside each region, such as Korea, Vietnam, India, Turkey, Brazil, Argentina and Nigeria, are a ranking from adoption studies, not measured holdings.

The chain data point the same way. $92.6B of USDT, 30% of all dollar stablecoins, sits on Tron, the cheap network used for payments in emerging markets. Chainalysis finds only $98B to $109B in personal wallets and ranks the US first in balances but 11th in cross-border flows. The IMF also finds that holdings rise about 75% within a year of a currency crisis and stay up.

No regulator publishes resident holdings. Brazil's central bank comes closest, because since February 2026 it books stablecoin trades as foreign exchange and reports that stablecoins are above 90% of crypto flows. The court upgrades Round 3's 'most supply is held abroad' from speculative to plausible, confidence 60.

v.g: Stablecoins are already a dollarization channel in weak-currency countries, which is why GENIUS reserve rules in US bills matter more abroad than at home.
v.b: The paying customer is the saver or importer in Lagos, Istanbul, Buenos Aires or Manila, not the US household.
v.p: If your currency has lost value, a dollar token is a cheap way to hold dollars. In the US it adds little over a bank account.

items.q: Next time Japan defends the yen, will it borrow through FIMA or sell Treasuries again?
a: It will most likely sell dollar securities again. Japan's own reserve data show both 2026 interventions were funded that way: the April to May operation (¥11.73T, about $75B) matched a $75.6B fall in foreign securities with deposits unchanged, and the July to August operation (¥15.40T, about $97B) matched an $87.8B fall in securities plus $6.9B of deposits. The desk gives about 80% that the next intervention is funded mainly by selling securities, bills first, and about 20% that the Fed's FIMA repo line is drawn above $1B during it.

FIMA was zero for 35 straight weeks from 18 February to 21 October 2026, even though Japan said on 3 August that it 'plans to utilize' it. The line is capped at $60B, below the size of either 2026 episode, and it charges a backstop rate. Japan still holds $821.7B of foreign securities and $154.8B of deposits with foreign central banks and the BIS (September 2026). Official selling paused in October: foreign official Treasuries in Fed custody rose $18.5B in the week to 21 October to a weekly average of $2,572.8B, down $176.0B on a year.

USD/JPY is about 156.8, below the 160 line where Japan acted twice, so the next test is not imminent (desk: any intervention by end 2026, 20). The 20% FIMA figure rises only if the Fed raises the cap and cuts the rate, or if Treasury market stress makes selling dearer than borrowing (conditional C9).

v.g: FIMA is a signal, not a funding tool, unless the Fed resizes it. Each yen defense adds supply to the Treasury market.
v.b: Expect long US yields to rise when Japan defends the yen, and treat a FIMA draw as the surprise.
v.p: A weak yen and Japanese sales of US bonds both feed slowly into US mortgage rates.

items.q: Do Gulf states get dollar lines from the Treasury, and on what conditions?
a: Not yet. Six months after the UAE raised a swap line with Treasury and Fed officials in April 2026, no US dollar line with any Gulf state has been announced. The Treasury's Exchange Stabilization Fund (ESF) statement for August 2026 lists only two agreements: Mexico ($9B, nothing drawn) and Argentina ($20B, a $2.5B swap in October 2025 fully repaid in December 2025). The Fed's swap lines stay with its five standing partners, with $170M outstanding on 21 October. Desk odds of a public US dollar line with a Gulf state: 7 by end 2026 and 20 by end 2028.

The ESF is smaller than its headline. Of its $218.8B of assets, $173.2B are Special Drawing Rights (SDRs), matched by $157.6B of SDR allocation liabilities and $15.2B of SDR certificates already issued to the Fed. Its net position is $44.3B and its dollar securities are $24.9B (court check of the statement). A Gulf line of real size would need more SDR certificates sold to the Fed, which the law allows only to finance exchange stabilization, or Fed participation.

Past conditions were hard. Mexico in 1995 got up to $20B, backed by its oil export proceeds and tied to an IMF programme with spending cuts, a small surplus, credit limits and data publication, and it repaid more than three years early with a net gain to the US of nearly $580M. Argentina's 2025 line was openly political, timed before its midterm elections. For the Gulf the stated aim is 'to prevent the sale of the US assets in a disorderly way', so the likely collateral is the Gulf's own Treasuries. Unstated conditions such as dollar oil pricing or limits on Chinese technology are decoded intent, graded D2, about 55.

v.g: Crisis dollars for non-core states are moving from technical Fed lines to political Treasury lines, but the Treasury has neither a large dollar balance sheet nor a signed Gulf deal.
v.b: The Gulf finances itself in markets ($102.7B of bonds and sukuk in the first half of 2026) and that will continue.
v.p: For people in the Gulf the dollar peg stays. A US line would be insurance for the central bank, not a change in your money.

items.q: Does conditional dollar access show up in central bank gold buying?
a: Partly, yes. The clearest sign is who buys. In 2026 the reported net buyers are central banks without a standing Fed swap line: China (about 101 tonnes from January to September, 23 straight months, 21 tonnes in September), Poland (98 tonnes to August), Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, the Czech Republic, Jordan, Malaysia, Ghana and the UAE. The five central banks with standing Fed lines bought nothing. The sellers are those most cut off from dollars or short of them: Russia (50 tonnes to July) and Turkey (85 tonnes to July). So conditional dollar access is one strong motive among several, not the whole story.

The World Gold Council's 2026 survey of 76 central banks adds motive and action: 90% cite gold's performance in crises, 85% of emerging-market respondents cite it as a geopolitical hedge, 74% expect the dollar's reserve share to be lower in five years, and 9% raised domestic storage in the past year (5% a year earlier). Moving gold home makes sense mainly if you fear a foreign custodian could freeze it.

Other motives matter. Poland is a NATO ally with full market access, and buying slows when prices are high (the first half of 2026 was the weakest since 2022 at 345 tonnes, then Q2 was 289 tonnes). The next checks are the WGC's Q3 data (desk 240 tonnes, 45% above 250) and the 2027 survey's storage answers (conditional C10).

v.g: Each time dollar access becomes political, through frozen reserves or conditional lines, the self-insurance demand for gold rises, and it shows first in where gold is stored.
v.b: Central bank demand is a durable bid, but it slows when prices are high.
v.p: Central banks buying gold signals distrust between governments, not a reason to swap your savings for bars.

items.q: Will China pair its solar know-how ban with yuan finance for the Global South?
a: Not explicitly, and so far only thinly. MOFCOM Announcement 2026 No. 48 (16 October) would ban or restrict 12 solar technologies and their core equipment, with comments due 15 November. Unlike its AI items, which get facilitation for members of a Chinese-led AI cooperation body, the solar part has no Global South clause. The pattern is 'sell the panels for cash, keep the factory know-how, and grow the yuan through debt management'. Desk odds: 20 that the final rule adds a solar facilitation clause for Global South partners, 30 that China announces a named yuan credit line tied to solar or green manufacturing exports by end 2027.

The yuan side is growing, but through refinancing and bonds rather than new solar loans. Chinese loan commitments to Africa were only $2.1B in 2024 with a single energy loan, but all of Kenya's 2024 infrastructure loans were in yuan. Panda bond issuance rose about 60% in the first half of 2026 to above RMB 160B, with first sovereign deals from Pakistan and Indonesia (RMB 7B).

The People's Bank of China (PBoC) now has 32 swap agreements worth about RMB 4.5T (about $672B), with RMB 132.8B (about $19.8B) drawn at end June 2026, up from RMB 79.3B in September 2025. That replaces the earlier single-source figure of RMB 3.84T across 42 central banks. The Fed's swap lines had $170M outstanding on 21 October, but the two serve different purposes.

v.g: Beijing keeps the technology lever and the currency lever separate, which lets it sell goods widely without giving away factories.
v.b: Expect cheap Chinese panels to keep flowing, line equipment and know-how to need licences, and yuan finance to be offered mainly on refinancing and bond deals.
v.p: Solar keeps getting cheaper where you buy Chinese panels for cash. A yuan loan for your country changes little for you unless your government struggles to earn yuan to repay it.

groups.title: France's rating, what official studies say about new residents, and where Europeans move
groups.intro: Moody's held France, and a one-notch cut would have mattered little. Official fiscal studies agree that route, age at arrival and earnings set the result. Europeans are not moving to Latin America or Southeast Asia in rising shares.

items.q: Will Moody's cut France, and does it matter?
a: Moody's did not cut. On 23 October 2026 it kept France at Aa3 with a negative outlook, against most analysts' expectations of a cut to A1, and said the rating assumes that a deficit-reducing 2027 budget will be adopted. A one-notch cut would have mattered little mechanically. What would matter is a slide of two agencies into the BBB band, which the court now treats as a scenario conditional (C11).

The mechanics explain why. Bond indices that use the middle of three ratings already see France at A+, the ECB's backstop (TPI) does not use ratings at all, and EU banks hold euro-area government debt in their own currency at a zero risk weight. History agrees: across 11 French downgrades since 2012 the France to Germany 10-year spread moved a median 4bp tighter from the month before to the month after. The one big widening, June 2024, came from the snap dissolution, not from the rating cut. Ratings follow spreads more than they lead them.

Scoring: the desk had 70 on 'Moody's or S&P downgrades France by 31 October' while a thin market priced 87.5 to 90.5. The contract settles on 31 October, and only an off-calendar S&P move could make it Yes, so it is recorded as a pending score. The court does not apply Round 4's 'no cut lowers H0 crisis odds by about 1 point': the hold is conditional, the spread was 171.8bp on 23 October against 130.3bp on 1 October, and the 2026 deficit slipped from 5.0% to about 5.4% of GDP. S&P reviews France next on 27 November.

v.g: The agencies grade the budget process, not the debt stock, so the 2027 finance bill and any use of Article 49.3 are the real rating events.
v.b: A one-notch move is noise for funding costs. The spread already prices worse than an A1 rating. The cliff to watch is the BBB band.
v.p: A rating cut does not change mortgage rates by itself. The 10-year yield does, and that is driven by the budget fight, the ECB and the 2027 election.

items.q: How much do new residents cost or contribute to European states?
a: Official studies find that the fiscal result depends mainly on the route of entry, age at arrival, and employment and earnings after arrival, and that method choices can change the sign of headline totals. Work routes are fiscally positive in every official study found, family routes lower, and humanitarian routes the most negative on fiscal accounts. Arrival in the 20s to about 30 gives the best lifetime result, because the host state did not pay for schooling and receives a full working life of taxes.

The UK Migration Advisory Committee (December 2025) finds the 2022/23 Skilled Worker cohort worth about +£47bn over its lifetime. Main applicants outside health and care average about +£689,000 each in present value, care workers about -£36,000 and adult dependants of health and care workers about -£67,000, against an average of -£39,000 for UK residents over their remaining lives. Denmark's Finance Ministry counted a net public cost of DKK 31bn in 2018 for immigrants and descendants from non-Western countries and a positive net contribution from immigrants from Western countries, and linked the difference mainly to the grounds of residence (asylum and family versus work). Australia's Treasury (2021, cited by the MAC) ranks its streams the same way: skill +A$198,000, family -A$126,000, humanitarian -A$400,000.

Totals move with method. In the MAC baseline even UK residents are negative on average because the base year ran a deficit, and the resident figure ranges from -£163,000 at a 1% discount rate to -£7,000 at 5%. How shared costs such as defence are split, whether children are counted, and who stays or leaves also change the result, so comparisons with residents on the same method are more informative than any single headline number. The UK fiscal watchdog (OBR, 2024) adds that an average-wage migrant arriving at 25 is more fiscally positive than a UK-born worker on the same wage, while low-wage profiles are negative over a lifetime.

v.g: The fiscal sign is set mostly by admission route and by labour-market access after arrival, so the levers are route design, faster work permission and recognition of qualifications, and these studies should be run regularly by official bodies with published methods.
v.b: Employer-sponsored routes are fiscally positive in every official study found, and the gain is concentrated in higher earners (in the UK, 72% of the Skilled Worker gain comes from the top 30% of earners).
v.p: The honest summary is 'it depends on the route, age and job'. Headline totals in either direction usually hide a method choice, above all how shared costs are split.

items.q: Are Europeans actually moving to Latin America or Southeast Asia in rising numbers?
a: No, not as a rising share. Slightly more people go in absolute numbers because total emigration rose, but in Eurostat's table of emigration by next country of residence for six EU countries with full detail (Italy, the Netherlands, Sweden, Belgium, Austria, Finland), Latin America took 4.5% of emigrants in 2019 and 4.1% in 2024, and Southeast Asia 1.6% in both years. Much of the Latin American flow is return migration or new citizens by descent going home. Intra-EU moves are over half of all emigration (53.8% in 2024).

For German citizens in 2025, Switzerland took 7.9%, the US 3.1% and Thailand 1.0% (2,894 people), while the four Latin American countries in the top 50 together took 1.1%. Southeast Asia in the top 50 took at least 5,175 Germans against at most about 5,000 for all of Latin America. Italy's statistics office says Latin America took almost 10% of Italian emigrants in 2023 to 2024, 'in part' new citizens returning home. So the court lowers Round 4's estimate that more Europeans (excluding heritage registrations) go to Latin America than to Southeast Asia from 75 to 45.

The fastest-rising non-European destination before the 2026 war was the UAE (0.4% to 0.9% of the six-country total from 2019 to 2024). Dubai's population fell 1.3% in March 2026 and was back above its pre-war level by mid-year, so the best reading is a shock and partial rotation, not a lasting exodus.

v.g: Europe's emigration goes mostly to its neighbours, Switzerland, the US and the Gulf, so talent policy should watch those channels, and statistics should separate returns and descent-citizens from native movers.
v.b: Latin America and Southeast Asia are niche destinations for European people (retirees, remote workers, heritage returns), not a talent-pool shift.
v.p: If you hear that 'everyone is moving to Mexico or Bali', official numbers say a few thousand a year per large country, while far more go to Switzerland, Spain or Austria.

groups.title: Housing supply, the human-made premium, dividend protections and the spread trade
groups.intro: Housing supply is shrinking under 7% mortgages. The human-made premium shows up as an AI discount. A new dividend would be less protected than Social Security unless the law says so. And borrowing at 6.19% to earn 13.6% mostly adds downside.

items.q: How fast can US housing supply actually respond in the 2020s?
a: Slowly, and in 2026 it is going backwards. Completions peaked at 1.627M in 2024, fell to 1.489M in 2025 and are running 12.5% below last year so far in 2026 (September annual rate 1.192M). Starts (1.221M) and permits (1.400M) say no rebound is coming soon. The desk's estimate of supply elasticity is about 1.0 nationally (range 0.5 to 1.75, coastal metros 0.3 to 0.8), which means new homes meet only about 5% to 10% of a demand shock within 3 years, 15% to 25% within 10 years and 25% to 40% within 20 years (model).

The brakes are price, not physics. The 30-year mortgage rate is 7.32%, about half of all mortgages carry 4% or less, so owners do not sell (existing supply 4.8 months), while builders sit on 8.5 months of new-home supply and cut starts. Input costs rose sharply in early 2026, and builders cite a shortage of about 300,000 construction workers. Factory-built homes are still 3% of single-family completions.

Zoning works where it is broad and by-right (Auckland, Austin) and narrow reforms deliver little. Mainstream shortage estimates cluster at 3.7M to 4.7M homes. Completions near 1.2M to 1.3M a year roughly match new households plus losses, so the gap is not closing. The court narrows Round 3's shelter supply input to 0.05 to 0.10 (now to 2028), 0.15 to 0.25 (2028 to 2035) and 0.25 to 0.40 (2035 to 2050), with 0.40 or more needing broad reform.

v.g: Rate cuts unlock existing homes, not new ones. Only by-right zoning plus faster permits moves the 20-year number, and it takes a decade to show.
v.b: Builders are destocking, so expect incentives and rate buydowns, not new starts, until mortgage rates fall below about 6.5%.
v.p: Do not wait for a building wave to fix rent where you live this decade. Your city's zoning votes set your price more than robot or factory news.

items.q: Is there a real cash premium for human-made goods?
a: Yes, but it is narrow, and the clearest money evidence shows a discount on AI-made goods rather than a measured premium on human-made ones. At the marketplace CGTrader, AI-made 3D models were about one in six uploads but 2.6% of sales and about $1 of every $90 of revenue (June 2025 to May 2026), so they sold less often and at lower prices, partly because of quality. No peer-reviewed, transaction-based estimate of the premium's cash size exists yet.

Experiments show a label effect: the same artwork is valued higher when labelled human-made, handmade lifts purchase intent mainly for gifts, and disclosing ads as AI-made cut clicks by up to 31.5% in a field test. Auctions show AI art sells when a known human stands behind it (Christie's Augmented Intelligence sale, $728,784). Stated surveys are louder than behaviour: 68% say they would pick human-made at the same price, yet readers paid the same for a story labelled AI-written.

Platforms that certify 'handmade' keep a growing slice: Etsy's take rate rose from 16.5% in 2019 to 24.2% in 2025 while its sales fell 5.3%. Proof decides who keeps the premium, so provenance rules matter more than robots.

v.g: The premium depends on proof, so provenance rules and penalties for false 'human-made' labels decide whether it reaches makers or fakers.
v.b: Sell the maker, the story, the gift and the service. Avoid putting 'AI' on the label of an emotional product, and expect platforms to tax the premium.
v.p: Human-made pays where buyers care who made it (gifts, art, care, personal services), not for commodity goods, where machines win on price.

items.q: If a UHI or AI dividend law passes, will payments be pledgeable or programmable?
a: Most likely neither pledgeable nor fully programmable, but less protected than people assume. US law decides benefit by benefit. Social Security payments cannot be assigned or garnished by private creditors (42 USC 407), but the rule that makes banks shield two months of deposited benefits (31 CFR 212) covers only Social Security, veterans, federal retirement and railroad payments, so a new AI dividend would get no automatic bank-account shield unless the statute or Treasury adds it. Desk odds for a federal cash AI dividend enacted by 2035: an anti-assignment clause 75, protection from private garnishment 55, still subject to child-support and federal-debt offsets 85, paid with spending restrictions 10, explicitly pledgeable 5.

Congress has chosen case by case. The 2021 advance child tax credit was protected from federal offsets but, per the IRS, not from state or private garnishment, while the December 2020 relief law shielded the second stimulus checks from private creditors. Alaska's dividend, the only US universal dividend, is only 20% exempt from creditors.

Programmability already exists without a central bank digital currency. SNAP benefits are spend-restricted on EBT cards and 22 states had waivers to bar soda or candy by March 2026. A retail Fed digital dollar is barred through 2030-12-31, so any token payment would ride private stablecoins, whose issuers must be able to freeze, seize or burn coins on lawful orders. No 2025 to 2026 AI dividend bill found addresses assignment or programmability.

v.g: Write anti-assignment, a bank-account shield and offset rules into the bill on day one, because the 2021 patchwork left families exposed to private garnishment.
v.b: The lending product will be underwriting against a dividend as income, not buying the stream, and stablecoin wallets will compete to receive deposits, not to restrict them.
v.p: Expect a dividend that cannot be sold or pledged and can be taken for child support or federal debts, and that a private creditor may be able to freeze at your bank unless the law says otherwise.

items.q: The newsletter spread trade: 'borrow at 6.19%, earn 13.6%'. What do volatility drag, sequence risk and margin calls do to it?
a: The spread is real on paper and mostly disappears once volatility, leverage and taxes are counted. Both legs are quoted at their best: 6.19% is Freddie Mac's 30-year mortgage rate a year ago (the same loan costs 7.32% today), and 13.6% matches the S&P 500's average for the ten years to 2022, above the 1928 to 2025 compound return of 10.0%. In the desk's model, borrowing half the position (a 50% loan) over 10 years leaves $100 of own money at a median of about $226 after tax against $216 unlevered, but the bad case (10th percentile) is about $38 against $107. The chance of at least one margin call is about 35% to 52% over 10 to 20 years at a 50% loan, and 8% to 18% at a 30% loan.

Volatility drag is the core problem. At 20% volatility a 13.6% average compounds at about 11.4% a year. Doubling exposure doubles volatility to about 40%, so the levered compound return is only about 11.7%, and at 25% volatility it is 6.8% against 10.1% unlevered (model). With interest added to the loan, a 50% position is called at a 65% loan-to-value after a 23% fall at the start, or after about 4.4 years even if prices go nowhere. Forced sales lock in losses, so the position cannot fully recover.

History is blunt. Starting at the 2000 or 2007 market peak, a 50% borrower was called and five years later held about $44 to $49 of every $100, while an unlevered investor held about $90 to $108. 19% of rolling 10-year windows since 1928 compounded below 6.19%. The trade clearly wins only in the calm, high-return world the 13.6% describes, at modest leverage (30% or less), with interest paid from income, over a horizon long enough to survive a 2000 or 2008.
This is general education about how leverage behaves, not personal financial advice.

v.g: Margin rules and lender calls force selling into crashes, which is why leveraged households amplify drawdowns.
v.b: Lenders earn either way (interest plus forced-sale fees), and portfolio lines float, so a hiking Fed raises the borrowing cost mid-trade.
v.p: Borrowing to invest roughly doubles the downside while adding only a little to the typical outcome. The model says small loans, interest paid from income and long horizons are what make it survivable.

groups.intro: The desk wrote 72 dated, scoreable predictions for the next weeks and months. The memory audit found the project's recalled figures mostly right, with six corrections already applied.

items.q: The next three weeks: what to watch, with dated, scoreable predictions
a: The desk wrote down 72 dated predictions before the events, each with a number and a resolution rule, to be scored with the Brier rule in a later round. The headline calls: the Fed holds on 28 October (91), Q3 GDP above 3.0% on 29 October (60), the ECB holds on 29 October (97), the French Assembly adopts the first part of its 2027 budget on 3 November (30), Treasury keeps coupon auction sizes unchanged on 4 November (85), the Lisa Cook hearing goes ahead with her taking part on 5 November (75), China issues a numbered extension of its export-control suspension by 10 November (72), and foreign official Treasury holdings fall in the September TIC data (90).

Further out: central bank gold demand above 250 tonnes in the WGC's Q3 report (45, point estimate 240), the dollar's share of reserves below 56.70% in the Q3 COFER data (80, point 56.2%), S&P cutting France below A+ by 30 November (25), the France to Germany spread above 150bp on 30 November (62) and above 200bp (12), a December Fed hike (70) and the 30-year mortgage rate above 7.00% at year end (70).

Market check: on every event with a market above $1M traded (the Fed decisions), the desk is within 15 points. The largest gap is on USDT reaching $200B by year end (desk 15, a thin market 42), because the coin has been flat for a year. One item is already resolved pending its score: Moody's held France on 23 October, so the desk's 70 against the market's 87.5 to 90.5 on a downgrade by 31 October will very likely score in the desk's favour on 31 October.

v.g: Writing predictions down before events is how a desk earns trust. The ledger will show whether the court's judgment beats thin markets.
v.b: The crowded window is 28 October to 10 November: the Fed, GDP and inflation, the ECB, the French vote, the refunding, the Cook hearing and China's deadline.
v.p: Most of these calls say 'no surprise'. The ones to watch for your own costs are the Fed in December and mortgage rates at year end.

items.q: Do the project's figures marked 'from memory' or 're-check' hold up?
a: Mostly yes. Of 52 memory-tagged items checked against primary or official sources, 38 are confirmed, 6 are corrected, 2 are confirmed but needed a precision fix, 1 is partly confirmed from a secondary source, and 5 stay unverifiable (three of them are funds that publish nothing, so 'estimate' is the right label). No published headline number or scenario odd changed.

The six corrections: China's CIC publishes total assets of $1.57T (end 2024), Saudi Arabia's PIF about $905B (2025, below the 'about $1T' shown), Hong Kong's Exchange Fund HK$4.15T (end 2025) and Temasek S$518B (March 2026), all four previously labelled as estimates or 'hundreds of billions'. The Winsemius mission to Singapore started in 1960, not 1961. And a lane figure was wrong: the German 10-year yield was about 2.4%, not 2.6%, at the start of 2025. These corrections were already applied.

All four decode items on the re-check list hold: the 1947 inflation peak was 19.7% (March 1947), the Bank of England bought £19.3B of gilts in 2022, the 1934 gold profit was about $2.8B with $2B to the ESF, and the legal gold cover on Federal Reserve notes ended on 18 March 1968. The lesson is a sourcing habit: label a size 'estimate' only after checking that the institution does not publish one.

v.g: The project's recall was accurate on dates and laws. Its weak spot was 'estimate' labels on numbers that institutions publish.
v.b: None of the corrections changes a decision. The PIF figure matters slightly for anyone sizing Gulf capital, because it is below $1T and fell in 2025.
v.p: The history in the Rulebook (gold, the 1940s yield cap, 2022 inflation, Malaysia 1998, crypto dates) can be trusted as written.
